text: Two men just short of thirty, and neither has settled what he is for. One lives on his parents' rural estate and lets the days pass; the other files copy in Düsseldorf without conviction behind it. Schonzeit für Füchse takes the harder route available to it: rather than hand either friend a crisis, it keeps them in each other's company and lets the distance between what they say and what they are doing widen on its own. Eighty-nine minutes is not much time for a film with this little event in it, and the compression tells - there is no room for the speech that would explain the pair to us. West Germany, 1966, and the friendship is the whole instrument. Berlin's jury gave it a Silver Bear Grand Jury Prize, which suggests the drift was read at the time as a decision rather than a failure of nerve.

The shooting has stopped, and the work that comes after it is burial. Five Chinese soldiers move across ground the Second Sino-Japanese War has finished with, putting bodies under earth and taking mines out of it, while somewhere ahead a starving Japanese unit has not been told the fighting is over. Wu Ziniu gives this ninety minutes and almost no plot; the situation supplies its own pressure, and it tightens with every hour the other side stays uninformed. What stands to be lost is not the war. It is whether men trained for years to kill can stop because a date has been announced. Berlin's jury gave it a Silver Bear Grand Jury Prize. The landscape does much of the arguing - ruin filmed at the pace of labour, without the swell that usually attends a victory.

Once a year a man goes back to the people he came from, and the visit is the entire design. His contemporaries are forty and prospering, arranged into a class that asks little of them at work and a great deal in the way of status; the annual return puts a witness in the room. Ulrich Schamoni's second feature works by ridicule rather than argument - German sentimentality is set up with some care and then declined outright. The performances hold it together where the satire slips, and some of what raises a laugh now was not built to raise one. It took a Silver Bear Grand Jury Prize in Berlin. Eighty-seven minutes, one recurring occasion, and a small circle of men at forty who have decided that comfort counts as an achievement.

In the north of Sweden a hunted man has two pursuers, and only one of them is a policeman. The other teaches school. That asymmetry is most of what ninety-four minutes of pursuit has to work with, along with the ground it crosses: country where distance is counted in hours and a figure ahead stays visible long after he is out of reach. Yngve Gamlin keeps the errand simple and the cast small. What a chase built this plainly tends to expose is not the fugitive but the two who agreed to go after him - the one doing his job, and the one who chose to come. Berlin's jury gave Jakten a Silver Bear Grand Jury Prize in 1965. The plainness looks less like modesty than like a wager: put three men in an emptiness and see what the pursuit turns into.

Going back to the place where a love began is a plan with the flaw built in, and the flaw is the subject. A photographer and the woman he cannot commit to return to the Italian town where they first met, walking the same streets deliberately, waiting for a feeling to arrive on schedule. Jealousy gets there first. Enzo Muzii runs it to eighty-four minutes in English, which puts a strange distance between the couple and the country they are moving through: a holiday conducted in a borrowed language. Shawn Phillips scores it on twelve-string guitar - acoustic, unhurried, atmosphere rather than comment. Berlin's jury gave it a Silver Bear Grand Jury Prize in 1968. What the film watches, patiently, is a man observing himself fail to feel what he came to feel.

A boy is left to himself in a nearly empty hotel, in a country whose language nobody in his family speaks and which is said to be close to war. Upstairs his mother and his aunt conduct a quarrel that never states its terms - one ill and bookish, the other going out into the town to find a man, both using the child as an instrument. Ninety-five minutes, three travellers, one building. Ingmar Bergman withholds the explanation a viewer keeps waiting for; nothing is translated, for the characters or for us, and the incomprehension is built into the structure rather than set in the way as an obstacle. It holds Sweden's Guldbagge for best film and a place on TSPDT's 1,000 Greatest Films. The unnamed country is not standing in for anything. It is a practical way of stranding people who already could not speak to one another.

It is 2019 in Los Angeles, the air unbreathable, and four manufactured people have come home to ask their maker for more life. Rick Deckard, retired from the work of killing them, is called back for one more round of it. The prizes went to production design, visual effects and cinematography - the crafts that build a world rather than the ones that tell a story, which is an honest account of where the weight sits. Ridley Scott shoots a detective picture at the tempo of a mood piece: 118 minutes of dread and looking, the plot mechanism running well below the surface of the image. It sits on the National Film Registry and in both Sight & Sound polls, the critics' and the directors'. What it keeps returning to is the term of a life - how long, decided by whom, and whether a made thing gets to negotiate.

Both of Apichatpong Weerasethakul's parents were doctors, and the hospital is where the family day took place. He makes that the material rather than the setting: the film is assembled out of what a child retained of adult routines he had no means to interpret - rounds, corridors, equipment, waiting. Slow cinema is the accurate label; the camera holds long after information has stopped arriving, and the holding is where the feeling collects. 105 minutes, in Thai. It carries a place on TSPDT's 1,000 Greatest Films and on the BBC's hundred best of the century, and a Lotus for best film. Very little of it behaves the way recollection is supposed to behave - nothing tinted, nothing underlined, and two doctors granted lives that were well under way before the person remembering them arrived.

Masako is the one nobody in the family looks at, until the day she kills her sister and has to disappear. What follows is not a manhunt. Junji Sakamoto spends two hours on the practical business of a woman with no social equipment having to build a life out of sight - work, rooms, the small negotiations she has never once conducted on her own behalf. The genre listing says crime and comedy, and both hold, uncomfortably: flight turns out to be the first thing she has ever been any good at. Kinema Junpo's critics named it the best Japanese film of its year and kept it on their list of the decade. It is a portrait of somebody becoming a person by the worst available route, filmed without much interest in whether that is forgivable.

The teacher's answer to a brawl between Japanese and Korean students is a friendly soccer match, and he sends two of the least qualified boys in class to carry the invitation. Kosuke has no stake in any of it - not a fighter, not a partisan - which is why the errand works on him: it puts him inside a community his own classmates have just insulted. The film took the Japan Academy Prize for picture, director and screenplay, and Kinema Junpo put it first among the year's releases. Kazuyuki Izutsu plays it broad, and the broadness is the tactic. Comedy at this volume can say plainly what the same material handled solemnly would route through metaphor: which language is spoken at home, whose city this is, what a border does when it runs through a school corridor.

The threat is a liquid: a potent new explosive, hijacked in transit by a North Korean special forces unit that means to force reunification on its own terms. Two agents of the South's intelligence service go after it, and after the unit's sniper, who has surfaced again after time away. Kang Je-kyu builds all of this with the full apparatus of an international action picture, surveillance and chases and a countdown, then points it at the one conflict where both sides hear their own language coming back at them. 125 minutes, and the pressure is not really coming from the bomb. Korea's Baeksang gave it best film and the Korean Film Archive put it on its list of a hundred. The genre machinery is imported wholesale; what it is aimed at is not.

The condition of their pardon is that they make the king laugh. Two street performers, arrested for a play that mocked him, are handed the palace as a stage and their own lives as the stake: an audience of one, absolute power in the seat, and the joke required to land. Lee Joon-ik spends two hours on the consequences of those terms. Satire that costs nothing in the street costs everything inside the walls, and the clowns' craft, which is the reading of a crowd, now has to work on a man nobody is permitted to read. Korea sent it to the Academy Awards as its submission and the Grand Bell named it best film. The pleasure is technical: watching people who are very good at something practise it in the one room where skill buys no protection.

A state assassination, filed under comedy, and the filing is correct. Im Sang-soo reconstructs the night of 26 October 1979 - the president who had run South Korea since 1961, and the intelligence director who worked for him - as an evening of rank, drink and improvisation carried out by men with no plan worth the name. 102 minutes for a few hours of history. The wager is that the events need no elevation: that the most consequential night the country had was conducted by people behaving exactly as small as they were, and that the indignity is the finding rather than a joke at history's expense. Baeksang named it best film, and the national archive holds it among a hundred Korean titles. What it withholds is solemnity, and the withholding amounts to a position on how power ends.

The method is not persuasion but attrition: sleep withheld, food withheld, a schedule with no hour left unaccounted for. A young man named David is taken in by a group that keeps its recruits hustling money in the street and lets exhaustion do the arguing on the leader's behalf. Ralph L. Thomas films this at something close to the speed it would take, and the patience is the whole argument - nothing supernatural occurs, and a person is disassembled by a timetable. The Academy of Canadian Cinema and Television named it best motion picture, and the National Board of Review placed it in the year's ten best. The tone throughout is procedural, nearer a case study than a warning, and the small concessions are left to accumulate without comment.
